1Illness script
Bottom line
  • A positive purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) with no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph is latent tuberculosis (TB) infection: not infectious, treated with a short rifamycin regimen.
  • Cough over 2 to 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss or an upper lobe cavity means active TB: airborne isolation first, then 3 sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT).
  • Treat active TB with four drugs, RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), for 2 months, then rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months; never one drug alone.
What it is

Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis: an asymptomatic latent stage often comes first, and in some it reactivates to active disease, most often in the lungs.

Bug

M. tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus: mycolic acids in its cell wall hold the stain. It lives inside macrophages and is walled off in granulomas.

Spread

Inhaled droplet nuclei from active pulmonary disease; a cavity holds the most bacteria and is the most contagious.

Reactivation risk: human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, the strongest; organ transplant drugs; glucocorticoids and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitors; silicosis; diabetes; dialysis.

Exposure risk: birth in or travel to a high-prevalence area, prison, a homeless shelter, substance use. Most new cases arise in Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific and Africa.

Chain

Inhaled bacilli

macrophages take them up but cannot fuse the phagosome with the lysosome

T cells build a caseating granuloma (

Skin testThe same delayed-type response makes the PPD skin test turn hard 48 to 72 hours after injection.

)

latent infection: test positive, chest film normal

immunity falls: reactivation, most often in the apices, where oxygen tension is high

upper lobe cavity: cough, night sweats, hemoptysis

Insights

No skin test or IGRA separates latent from active TB; the symptoms and the chest radiograph do.

TNF-α holds the granuloma together, so a TNF-α inhibitor can let latent TB reactivate; screen before the first dose.

FindingAction

DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Reactivation (secondary) pulmonary TBCough over 2 to 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis; upper lobe infiltrate or cavityAirborne isolation, then 3 sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and NAAT.

4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Health care worker: negative first PPD, positive on a repeat 1 to 3 weeks laterA boosted old infection, not a recent conversionTreat it as latent infection once symptom review and CXR are clear.
Positive PPD after a BCG vaccine given abroad (not used in the United States)Count it as true infection In practice: the BCG effect on the skin test usually wanes after several years, and an IGRA avoids the question.Proceed as for any positive test: symptom review and CXR.
HIV with a CD4 count under 200, fever, old age or heavy immunosuppressionAnergy: a negative PPD does not exclude TBPrefer an IGRA; do not rely on a negative skin test.
Pause point
A month of cough, night sweats and an upper lobe cavity on the CXR Offered as start RIPE now or send sputum and wait Isolation comes before any drug or sputum result → Airborne isolation in a negative-pressure room
A positive IGRA, no symptoms, a normal CXR Offered as repeat the IGRA or four drugs No test separates latent from active; the film and symptoms do → Latent TB: a rifamycin regimen (step 7)
5Diagnostic criteria
Latent infection versus active disease
StateCriteria
Latent TB infectionPositive PPD or IGRA and no symptoms and a normal CXR; not infectious
Active TBSymptoms or a CXR suggesting TB; confirmed by AFB smear, NAAT or culture
PPD cutoffs by risk group
IndurationGroup
5 mm or moreHIV; recent contact of an active case; fibrotic changes of old TB on CXR; organ transplant; TNF-α inhibitor; prednisone ≥15 mg/day for over 1 month
10 mm or moreInjection drug use; immigrant within 5 years from a high-prevalence area; prison or homeless shelter; health care worker; diabetes; silicosis; In practice: some references place end-stage kidney disease on dialysis at 5 mm.; child under 4
15 mm or moreNo risk factors
6Severity
What changes the regimen
FindingMeaning
Cavity on the first CXR and a positive culture at 2 monthsIsoniazid and rifampin for 7 more months: 9 months in all
HIV with active TBTB drugs first; antiretroviral therapy (ART) after 2 weeks, to lower the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; rifabutin in place of rifampin with protease inhibitors
HIV with latent TB, on interacting ARTIsoniazid with vitamin B6 for 9 months; rifamycins interact with ART
7Treatment
1

Latent TBPositive test, no symptoms, normal CXR

Isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 3 months, or rifampin daily for 4 months, both first line; isoniazid daily for 9 months only if neither can be taken.

2

Active TB, first 2 monthsSymptoms or an abnormal CXR; drug susceptible

RIPE, started promptly once the patient is isolated, without waiting for cultures.

3

ContinuationAfter 2 months

Stop pyrazinamide and ethambutol; rifampin and isoniazid for 4 more months, 6 months in all.

4

Hepatitis on treatmentSymptoms of hepatitis

Stop isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide; restart them one at a time.

RIPE toxicities by drug
DrugToxicityDo
RifampinRed-orange urine, sweat and tears; strong cytochrome P450 inducer: oral contraceptive and warfarin failure; hepatitisCounsel, do not stop it; switch the contraceptive; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy from vitamin B6 loss; hepatitis; drug-induced lupus; sideroblastic anemia; seizuresVitamin B6 for those at risk; stop it for symptomatic hepatitis
PyrazinamideHyperuricemia, often; gout, rarely; hepatitisUsually mild; the drug stops after 2 months
EthambutolOptic neuritis: In practice: a major reference describes trouble telling blue from green first; acuity may then fall., then acuityBaseline color vision and acuity, then monthly vision questions; substitute another drug if it occurs
8Follow-up
After the diagnosis
WhenDo
Every active caseNotify the health department, which traces close contacts.
Close contacts of an active casePPD or IGRA now; repeat a negative test 8 to 10 weeks after the exposure; a close-contact child under 5 is treated even if negative.
HIV, psychiatric illness, substance use, poor adherenceDirectly observed therapy: a public health worker watches each dose.
Leaving airborne isolationUsually 3 negative sputum smears over 2 days, at least 1 early-morning sample.
On isoniazid, rifampin or pyrazinamideReturn for fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting or jaundice; liver tests then, not routinely unless liver risk factors.
Mother with active, untreated TBBreastfeeding is contraindicated until it is treated.
Practice
  1. Booster / two-step: health care worker with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion → Treat as latent
  2. Window period: contact of an active case → PPD now and at 8–10 weeks → the only time "repeat later" is correct
  3. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease stem) → Screen for latent TB first
  4. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR → Airborne isolation → before any medication is started
